title: Asado
subtitle: argentine slow-grilled beef ribs
excerpt: Argentine slow-cooked beef shin or ribs, rubbed simply with garlic, herbs and black pepper and grilled low and slow until tender. Served with chimichurri.
sourceNotes: Asado is the Argentine tradition of slow-cooking beef over wood embers. This griddle-pan version captures the key elements at home: long, gentle heat and minimal interference.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Rub the beef 4 hours ahead and refrigerate uncovered for better surface drying before cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Argentine tradition of slow-cooking beef over embers or a wood fire.

content.text: is a philosophy as much as a cooking method. The meat is treated with respect and cooked slowly. No marinades. No sauces during cooking. Just good beef, time, low heat and confidence. The seasoning is applied dry, and the crust that forms is where all the flavour lives.
Beef shin is used here because it becomes tender and deeply flavourful over a long cook. Use a thermometer to check doneness rather than guessing.
Pat the beef dry with kitchen paper. Mix together the garlic paste, olive oil, thyme, rosemary and cracked black pepper. Rub all over the beef pieces. Leave at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Heat the griddle pan over medium heat. Do not get it smoking hot. Place the beef pieces on the griddle and cook undisturbed for 15 minutes.
Turn using tongs. Cook for another 15 minutes. Continue turning every 15 minutes over medium-low heat for a total of 75 to 90 minutes.
Check with an instant-read thermometer. Beef shin is best at 90C internal temperature, where the collagen has fully broken down. The meat should be very tender and pulling away from the bone.
Rest for 10 minutes before serving. Serve with chimichurri and lemon wedges alongside roasted peppers and crusty bread.

attrs.issue: Outside charring before the inside is tender

content.text: Lower the heat. Asado requires patience and medium-low heat throughout. After an initial sear, keep the heat low so the inside cooks gently while the outside stays intact.

attrs.issue: Meat is still tough after 90 minutes

content.text: Transfer to a 160C oven and continue cooking for another 30 minutes. Shin needs time and moist heat to break down. Adding a splash of water to the roasting tin helps.
The beef surface may have been damp. Pat it completely dry before rubbing. Increase the heat slightly for the first 5 minutes of each side to set the crust.

Asado is the social centre of Argentine life. It is cooked on weekends, at family gatherings and at national holidays. The asador, the person who tends the fire, is a position of honour. Argentina has one of the highest per-capita beef consumption rates in the world. The gaucho tradition of cooking over open wood fire dates back centuries. Today, an asado can last an entire afternoon.
